title: Academic writing
text:
I have authored over 50 journal articles, as well as a range of other output. Here, I categorize all this into two broad areas of my work (global governance & international political economy; and global health & social protection), and flag my favourite articles with an emoji (🥰).
The most up-to-date list of publications is available on my Google Scholar profile.

title: About
text:
⬇ Download CV (PDF)
I am a social scientist working at the intersection of political economy, international relations, and sociology. My research asks two connected questions: how are the rules of the global economy made, and what do they do to people?

title: About
text:
Research
The first strand of my work opens the black box of decision-making in global governance. Globalisation means organisation: the integration of markets has been accompanied by a proliferation of rules, norms, and bureaucracies governing the activities of states, firms, and citizens. I study how these rules emerge, who writes them and how they are contested. My research also reveals how political pressures and expert knowledge interact in producing the policy scripts that international organisations promote around the world. Much of this work relies on original data that make otherwise opaque institutions open to systematic analysis.
The second strand of my research examines the consequences of globally devised policies for health and social protection. My early work on the Greek crisis was among the first to document how austerity was damaging population health. This developed into a comparative programme built around the most comprehensive dataset of policy conditions attached to IMF agreements (developed with Thomas Stubbs and available on www.imfmonitor.org). The findings show how these reforms can weaken state capacity, increase corruption, and widen income and health inequalities. More recently, I have examined the development and impact of policies underpinning the global green transition and health system preparedness.
Across these projects, I combine archival research, quantitative methods, computational text analysis and interviews. Overall, the different strands of my work have attracted more than €1 million in research funding.

title: About
text:
Policy engagement
I treat research and policy as closely connected. I have presented my findings at the IMF-World Bank Annual and Spring Meetings, the G20 Working Group on International Monetary Architecture, the UN Human Rights Council and the European Parliament, and have produced policy research for the World Health Organization, Oxfam International, the Recourse Foundation and the Foundation for European Progressive Studies. I serve on the Lancet Commission on Global Governance for Health and on the WHO’s expert group on the economics of health and wellbeing. From 2020 to 2024, I was Vice-President of Greece’s National Centre for Social Solidarity.

title: About
text:
Academic leadership and service
At Bocconi, I direct the PhD Programme in Social and Political Sciences, with responsibility for its academic development, admissions, doctoral training, mentoring and placement. I also coordinate the Politics and the Welfare State research unit at the Dondena Centre for Research on Social Dynamics and Public Policy, an interdisciplinary group bringing together scholars working on political decision-making, public policy, inequality and social protection.
A further part of my institutional work takes place through CIVICA, the European University Alliance of leading social science institutions. I oversee Master’s-level activities across the alliance, including multi-campus courses, intensive seminars, digital mobility and jointly delivered teaching. I also represent Bocconi on CIVICA’s scientific committee, which develops collaborative research, faculty-mobility and funding initiatives across its member institutions.
Beyond Bocconi, I contribute to the wider academic community through editorial, funding-evaluation, and advisory roles. I serve on the editorial boards of several journals, evaluate scholarship applications for the Onassis Foundation, and sit on the advisory board of the History and Political Economy Project.

title: Alexandros Kentikelenis
text:
I am Professor of Political Economy and Sociology at Bocconi University in Milan, where I direct the PhD Programme in Social and Political Sciences and coordinate the ‘Politics and the Welfare State’ research unit at the Dondena Centre. I am a scholar of global governance, studying how international cooperation is sustained under pressure and how international organisations develop and diffuse policies that shape social protection and inequality around the world. Before moving to Milan, I held research posts at Oxford, Cambridge and Harvard.
I have co-authored four books, most recently How Europe Survives: The Adaptability and Resilience of a Continent in Peril (Oxford University Press, 2026, with Catherine De Vries) and Making Global Norms: Politics versus Science in International Organizations (Oxford University Press, 2025, with Leonard Seabrooke), which received the American Society of International Law’s prize for the best book on international law and social science. My earlier books, Greening the International Monetary Fund and A Thousand Cuts: Social Protection in the Age of Austerity (both with Thomas Stubbs), draw on the largest database of IMF-mandated reforms to trace their consequences for public services and inequality. My academic articles have appeared in leading journals, including the American Journal of Political Science, the American Journal of Sociology, the American Sociological Review, The Lancet and World Development. My research has received multiple professional awards, including the 2024 Henrik Enderlein Prize for Research Excellence in the Social Sciences.
Beyond academia, I work closely with policymakers and civil society. I serve on the Lancet Commission on Global Governance for Health and on the World Health Organization’s expert group on the economics of health and wellbeing. Over the years, I have advised governmental, intergovernmental, and non-governmental organisations, including Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Cooperation and Development, the World Health Organization, Recourse Foundation, and Oxfam International. Between 2020 and 2024 I was Vice-President of Greece’s National Centre for Social Solidarity.
I have also written regularly for a wider public, including in the New York Times, the Washington Post, the Guardian and Kathimerini, and my work has been covered by major international press outlets.

title: Books
text:
With Catherine E. De Vries · 2026 · Oxford University Press (code AUFLY30 for 30% off)

How Europe Survives: The Adaptability and Resilience of a Continent in Peril challenges the familiar narrative of European decline and perpetual crisis. Instead of treating the EU as a machine in need of constant repair or as a project forever on the verge of collapse, the book reframes Europe as a living organism: imperfect, evolving, and capable of absorbing shocks without breaking apart. Building on a sweeping reinterpretation of European integration from the post-war decades to the turbulence of the 2020s, How Europe Survives argues that the EU’s hallmark features—its multiple veto points, overlapping institutions, and endless negotiations—are surprising sources of resilience that have repeatedly confounded predictions of collapse.


Praise


“A timely and thought-provoking reflection on the continent’s past, present and future. An essential read for defenders of Europe.” — Enrico Letta, former prime minister of Italy


“Lately it has been very popular to bash Europe and criticise its lack of action in an increasingly turbulent world. This book by de Vries and Kentikelenis offers a different perspective. It shows that the European Union, since its creation, has indeed been a very adaptive organism and has remained resilient throughout decades of crises because of its flexibility. Therefore, also in this era of polycrisis, there is hope—if there is enough political will.” — Cecilia Malmström, former European Commissioner for Trade, and for Home Affairs


“European integration has been under strain for years, facing shock after shock. De Vries and Kentikelenis invite the reader to explore different dimensions of this crisis, including geopolitical and social. They rebut the habitual doomsayers not through citations of institutional optimism but by highlighting the EU’s adaptive strength and its genuine chance to build effective sovereignty.” — László Andor, former European Commissioner for Employment, Social Affairs and Inclusion


“This is one of the most original and compelling books on Europe’s future in years. De Vries and Kentikelenis move beyond the tired opposition between European decline and federalist salvation to offer a new way of thinking about the Union. By recasting Europe as an adaptive organism, they illuminate how conflict, compromise and imperfection can become sources of resilience. A brilliant and accessible account for anyone concerned with the European project.” — Kalypso Nicolaïdis, European University Institute


“De Vries and Kentikelenis explain how Europe has adapted to survive, and why today’s security and economic challenges will demand more than muddling through. A bracing and timely agenda for action, and essential reading for scholars and practitioners alike.” — Simon Hix, London School of Economics


“Too much has been written about the EU against an unrealistic template — one that sets the bar so high the institution is declared dead or irrelevant with exhausting regularity. How Europe Survives offers a brilliant corrective: an account of how the EU endures—imperfectly, but durably—that recalibrates the very yardsticks by which we judge it.” — Stephanie C. Hofmann, Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies


“This is exactly the book we need right now. De Vries and Kentikelenis compellingly show how the complexity, imperfections, and resilience of the European Union are a feature not a bug—and surprising sources of strength and adaptation in today’s challenging world. This creative and deeply thoughtful book is a must-read for anyone interested in a more prosperous, secure, and democratic Europe.” — Kathleen R. McNamara, Georgetown University

title: Teaching & students
text:
Prospective PhD students
What I am open to supervising. Highly ambitious projects in international and european political economy; global health governance; global social protection; and the political economy of the green transition. I am very open in terms of methodological approaches (my work relies on both quantitative and qualitative methods), provided they are appropriate to answer the research questions being investigated.
How to get in touch. As I am the director of the Bocconi PhD in Social and Political Sciences, I sit on the admissions committee and therefore cannot offer detailed advice or guidance on your research ideas. So, as long as your interests align with mine, you can assume that I am in principle available to supervise. Confirmation by a supervisor that they are interested in working with you is not necessary at the application stage. Bocconi has many leading academics who are available to supervise PhD students, so you should take a close look at whose work might be the best fit with your research interests. Any questions about the Bocconi SPS PhD program should be directed to phd.sps@unibocconi.it.

title: Policy
text:
I am keen to facilitate the take-up of my academic research by policymakers. To this end, I collaborate extensively with international organisations and civil society to reach broader policy audiences.
